ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Amoebiasis is an intestinal infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, often progressing to liver abscesses. Diagnosis relies on stool microscopy, antigen tests, and imaging. Treatment combines a tissue‑acting drug with a luminal agent.

sections.p: Amoebiasis is caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, transmitted via fecal‑oral route. Diagnosis starts with stool microscopy for trophozoites or cysts, confirmed by antigen detection or PCR. Imaging (ultrasound or CT) identifies liver abscesses.

t.b: Detects E. histolytica antigens; positive means active infection, negative does not exclude if low parasite load.
Highly sensitive; confirms species, useful when microscopy is equivocal.
Shows hypoechoic liver lesions; helps differentiate abscess from cysts.

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom intensity and organ involvement. Mild disease is self‑limited dysentery; moderate involves liver abscess; severe includes septic shock or multi‑organ failure.
Primary cause is ingestion of contaminated food or water. Risk factors include poor sanitation, HIV, malnutrition, and concurrent intestinal infections.
Patients report abdominal pain, bloody or mucoid stool, fever, and weight loss. Liver abscess presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and sometimes jaundice.
Lab tests confirm infection and assess complications. Imaging guides management of abscesses.
Complications include abscess rupture, septicemia, and intestinal perforation. Red flags are sudden severe pain, high fever, or signs of shock.

Treat with a tissue‑acting nitroimidazole (e.g., metronidazole) followed by a luminal agent (e.g., paromomycin) to eradicate cysts. Supportive care includes fluids and antibiotics for secondary infections.
Repeat stool microscopy to confirm cure. Prevent by ensuring clean water, hand hygiene, and safe food handling. Vaccines are not available.
Amoebic colitis can mimic bacterial dysentery, ulcerative colitis, or ischemic colitis. Liver abscess may resemble pyogenic abscess or cystic lesions.
Microscopy may miss cysts in low parasite load; antigen tests can cross‑react with non‑pathogenic Entamoeba species; imaging may misinterpret cysts as abscesses.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain, high fever, signs of shock, jaundice, or inability to tolerate oral intake

faq.a: Yes, many carriers have no symptoms but can still spread the parasite.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for amoebiasis?
faq.a: No, there is currently no vaccine available.
Recurrence is possible if cysts are not fully eradicated; repeat stool testing helps ensure cure.
